geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately preserves the intended region structure: the two filled subregions are bounded by the top line and the appropriate lower line, the endpoints are computed from the intersections with y = 3, and the top boundary and side boundaries update to those limits. concept.rationale: Both figures correctly show the default triangular region with vertices (-2,3), (0,1), and (2,3), the top boundary y=3, the lower boundaries y=-x+1 and y=x+1, and the split into R1 and R2 at the y-axis for type-I integration (L00007-L00011, L00025-L00036, L00040). geometry.rationale: Figure 1 much more accurately reconstructs the textbook structure: it preserves the three molecular snapshots across the top plus two stacked panels for concentration and rate, with panel labels, arrowed axes, dashed equilibrium line, shaded equilibrium region, and curves that plateau after equilibrium. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is clearly recognizable as the textbook figure, with the three molecular beaker panels and the two concentration/rate graphs using similar red/blue curves, labels, dashed equilibrium markers, and shaded equilibrium regions. labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes most of the key labels from the reference, such as t = 0, pre-equilibrium, at equilibrium, N2O4, NO2, Concentration, Rate, Time, panel labels, and equilibrium annotations, though some are small and slightly cluttered. concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the core equilibrium concepts: [N₂O₄] decreases, [NO₂] increases, both plateau in the equilibrium region, and the forward rate k_f[N₂O₄] decreases while the reverse rate k_r[NO₂]^2 increases until they become equal and remain constant (L00012, L00023). Figure 1 also preserves the three-stage molecular progression from colorless N₂O₄ to a brown mixture at equilibrium better than Figure 2’s single time-dependent snapshot (L00018, L00023).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is decisively stronger: it preserves the textbook layout with three molecular snapshots plus separate concentration and rate panels, includes the key labels and equilibrium annotations, and represents the chemistry correctly with concentrations plateauing and forward/reverse rates becoming equal. Figure 2 is much weaker visually and conceptually, reportedly rendering only an error in screenshot-based review and, in its source behavior, collapsing the structure into a simplified single-view interaction whose curves continue changing through the marked equilibrium region and show unequal rates at the claimed equilibrium time.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 more closely preserves the likely textbook geometry: a 6×6×6 input lattice, a single channel-spanning row of six weight cubes, a 6×6 output sheet, and an oblique front/depth projection with the highlighted receptive slice aligned to one output element. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it preserves the original left-to-right composition with a clean input layer, central weight blocks, output layer, labels, dimension arrows, and the grey selected band in roughly the same arrangement. labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the required diagram labels (Width, Height, Channels, Input layer H, Weights Ω, Output layer H′) placed clearly and readably near the corresponding elements, whereas Figure 1’s labels are crowded, overlap the artwork and each other, and include extra invented annotations such as selected output channel text and a formula that clutter the figure. concept.rationale: Figure 1 more truthfully represents a multi-channel 1D convolution: its labels and status text assert that Ω combines all input channels across k width positions to form a selected channel of H′, and it shows output width W′ = W − k + 1, which matches the brief’s requirement that the layer be a weighted linear combination across channel and spatial dimensions with multiple output channels (L00007). Figure 2 instead asserts that the learned weight array is applied only across the channel dimension to produce a single output feature channel, and its weight tensor is just a length-6 channel vector with no spatial kernel width or multiple output-channel filters, so it would teach an incorrect reduction of the multi-channel 1D convolution described in the brief (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the stronger overall match to the referenced diagram: it preserves the 6×6-style geometry, left-to-right layout, selected band, and clear labels much better than Figure 1, whose rotated view, crowded annotations, and invented extra elements make it less visually faithful and harder to read. geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the detailed U-Net geometry: it includes the full symmetric 19-block sequence, repeated residual blocks at each resolution, five skip connections, full-resolution input/output slabs, and timestep injections to all blocks with spatial sizes scaled consistently by resolution and channel depth. Figure 2 has a cleaner oblique presentation, but it collapses the architecture into only 13 feature volumes, omits several repeated blocks/bottleneck elements, uses fewer timestep injections, and appears to misplace or overuse self-attention highlights, making its reconstructed geometry less faithful overall.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the requested interactions much more correctly: Prev/Next and play actually advance through named encoder-bottleneck-decoder states, skip connections pulse on the corresponding decoder reuse step, the speed control affects playback, the timestep slider updates a readout and moves/attenuates tracers along the time-embedding and injection paths, and the attention toggle visibly enables/disables attention highlighting. Figure 1 has working basic handlers, but its timestep slider only triggers a generic fading color pulse that is not tied to the slider value and has no readout, and its data-flow animation is a simple continuous loop with no step control or explanatory state; its skip pulsing and attention highlighting work, but less completely and less accurately than Figure 2.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable as the original U-Net-style architecture: it preserves the grey input/output panels, brown 3D feature blocks with decreasing/increasing sizes, diagonal time-embedding arrows, skip/concatenate connections, and legend-like annotation. labels.rationale: Figure 2 has larger, more readable labels for the main annotations such as the tensor sizes, 'Concatenate', and 'time embedding', whereas Figure 1’s labels are generally very small, angled into the perspective view, and many central labels are nearly illegible due to overlap. concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the key U-Net relationships: its skip connections labeled “Concatenate” link encoder and decoder blocks at matching spatial scales such as 256→256, 128→128, 64→64, 32→32, and 16→16, matching the brief’s requirement for skip connections at matching scales (L00007). Both figures convey the encoder-decoder/downsample-upsample structure, timestep conditioning, and residual/self-attention legend reasonably well (L00007), but Figure 2’s false skip-scale relationships make it less conceptually accurate.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it preserves the intended U-Net architecture more faithfully: it shows the fuller symmetric block sequence, matching-scale skip concatenations, repeated resolution stages, timestep injections, and the recognizable textbook-style input/output and feature-volume layout. Those architectural and conceptual errors outweigh Figure 2’s interaction and labeling advantages.
